title: Draupadi
hook: the man who killed her sons in their sleep is dragged before her in ropes, and in the Bhagavata's telling she asks for him to be set free

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi and the empty pot: Krishna arrived hungry and made a meal of one leaf on the rim. Did you find something small left to give? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-four.

Ropes around his arms, Ashvatthama is pushed forward and made to stand in front of her. He is the son of Drona, the Pandavas' own teacher. And on the last night of the war he crept into their sleeping camp and killed Draupadi's sons. Arjuna has caught him and tied him up like an animal. Krishna has told Arjuna he may kill him. Instead, Arjuna brings him to the mother of the dead. Draupadi looks at him. Last year on this path, the Mahabharata's telling of this moment ended with a jewel. Today, the Bhagavata Purana tells it, and she says something else.
screen: `THE KILLER, IN ROPES.` → `BROUGHT TO THE MOTHER.` → `THE BHAGAVATA TELLS IT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana's first book, Draupadi sees the son of her husbands' teacher bound and ashamed, and she bows to him. Then she speaks, here in paraphrase. Let him go. Let him go. He is the son of the teacher from whom you learned your bows and your weapons. In him, the teacher is still here. And then the line the whole scene turns on. His mother, Kripi, is still alive. Don't let her weep the way I am weeping now. The text calls her words fair, kind and full of dharma, and it says some of those present agree with her. Bhima does not. He says this man killed sleeping children and deserves to die. Krishna finds a way through. Arjuna cuts the jewel from Ashvatthama's head and shaves his hair, a punishment the text treats as a kind of death for one like him, and sends him out of the camp alive. Now set the two tellings side by side, without ranking them. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi refuses food until she sees the jewel taken from his head. In the Bhagavata, she asks for his life. Readers have held both. Look closely at what she does and doesn't do. Her grief doesn't vanish; she names it, I am weeping. Her mercy doesn't excuse him; the punishment still falls. And the reason she gives is another mother. She doesn't ask what he deserves. She asks who else will be sitting where she is sitting tonight.
screen: `SHE BOWS TO THE BOUND MAN` · `HE IS OUR TEACHER'S SON` · `LET HIS MOTHER NOT WEEP AS I DO` · `TWO TELLINGS, BOTH HELD`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the other mother. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who hurt you, small or large. You don't have to forgive them in this sit. Draupadi's mercy doesn't erase the harm, and nobody is asked to. Just look past the person, once, to someone who loves them: a mother, a child, a friend. Let that person be there for a few breaths. Notice what changes in you, if anything. If you pray, you can hold that other person in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi. In the Bhagavata, with her sons' killer in ropes before her, she asks for his life so that his mother won't weep as she does. Today's word.
Your line: Draupadi. Today, when someone annoys or hurts you, think once of a person who loves them, the way Draupadi thought of Kripi. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Hindus who read or hear the Bhagavata Purana meet this scene early in its first book, sometimes in long public recitations, and storytellers set it beside the Mahabharata's own telling.

match.prompt: the man in ropes — tap the pairs.
pairs: son of Drona, the Pandavas' teacher

myth: in the Bhagavata, Draupadi demands Ashvatthama's death
in the Bhagavata she asks for his life; in the Mahabharata she asks for the jewel from his head.
Draupadi's reason is that his mother should not weep as she does
she names Kripi, and her own weeping.
Ashvatthama walks free with no punishment at all
his jewel is cut away and his hair shaved, and he is sent out of the camp.

fork.setup: you're Draupadi. the man who killed your sons stands bound before you, and your husband waits for your word. what do you say?
options: let him go; his mother still lives.
fork.reveal: in the Bhagavata she bows to him and asks for his release, so that Kripi won't weep as she does. the punishment still falls, but he lives.

original.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, Drupada's daughter, the woman who asks for mercy in the Bhagavata's telling.

trapdoor: what you thought: Draupadi is a figure of anger and revenge.
what it means: in the Bhagavata, she bows to her sons' killer and asks for his life.
what a scholar hears: the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata tell this scene differently, and tradition keeps both.

notes: Confirm the Bhagavata 1.7 paraphrase: Draupadi bows to Ashvatthama; asks for his release because he is the guru's son and Drona lives on in him; asks that Kripi not weep as she does; the text praises her words; Bhima objects; Krishna's resolution; Arjuna removes the jewel and shaves his head, which the text treats as a death-equivalent punishment for a brahmin.
